<p>Útil quando uma pista só entra a toca:

= cursor: choose the bar, play/pause exactly where it should sound, and click — the chosen bar (and everything after it) lines up with the cursor.

Tempo (bar BPM): type the BPM the bar should have (it comes filled in with the current one) and, if you like, up to which bar to apply it — they all take that BPM. What comes after does not change tempo: it only shifts by the difference, so each following bar keeps its own. Like the other sync tools, it creates a pending correction per track — saved with "Apply and rebuild".
<p>Se a tabulatura e a gravação se vão a: If the tab and the recording drift further apart as the song goes on (the GP was written at a slightly different tempo from the one recorded), adjust the tempo: it stretches/compresses the whole song in one go. The notes move over the waveform so you can confirm the alignment.
<p>Deteta o andamento e o início da grav:
Detects the tempo and the start of the recording (like CDLC.AI) and proposes an adjustment. The values stay in preview — confirm them on the score and click "Apply and rebuild".
Important tip: if you have already run "Separate instruments", tempo detection is done on the isolated drums — much more reliable on fast, dense music (on the full mix, the beat detector gets the metrical level wrong). Separate first for a much better result.
Requires the ml extra (librosa). Refine afterwards with the manual modes.
<p>A sincronização automática acima apli:
The automatic sync above applies ONE average tempo — not enough when the recording's tempo varies (the typical problem with AI tabs). This one follows the real tempo curve: it uses the beat grid for the local tempo, and fine-tunes each anchor by fitting the tab's own notes onto the audio's attacks.
Run "Separate instruments" first: the beat grid then comes from the isolated drums and the attacks from the isolated guitar — much more reliable than the full mix (where the beat detector gets the tempo wrong). Without separation, it uses the mix and warns you.
Start at the first note: set the start in Step 1 first (or with "🎯 Detect 1st note") — the first anchor is exactly that point and the alignment applies from there on.
It replaces the current track's pending corrections with this proposal; it stays in preview — see the ♩BPM per bar on the score (amber = changed by the anchors) and confirm with "Apply and rebuild".
Honest limit: sections where the tab's notes do not match the audio are flagged with ⚠ — there the problem is the tab's content (wrong notes/bars), which no sync can fix; fix those parts in Guitar Pro. Requires the ml extra (librosa).
<p>Escreve as correções de <b>andamento<:
Writes the tempo corrections you accepted into a copy of your Guitar Pro file, so the fix becomes permanent in Guitar Pro itself and not only in RockForge. Your original file is never changed.
Everything else is preserved: notes, techniques, tuning, tracks, sections, lyrics — and the tempo changes you wrote yourself survive too.
Formats: .gp3/.gp4/.gp5 and .gp (GP7/8). .gpx (GP6) is not written by any tool — not even Guitar Pro exports to it; export as GP5 or GP7 first.
Honest limit: the binary formats (gp3/4/5) store the tempo as a whole number, so 119.085 becomes 119 — we always tell you what was actually written. .gp keeps the decimals.
Tempo only: a jump cannot be expressed as a BPM change (it would need a bar inserted/removed), so it does not go into the file — fix that one in Guitar Pro.
<p>Não corrige nada — <b>diagnostica</b>:
It fixes nothing — it diagnoses. All the other tools answer "where should each note go"; this one answers "what kind of problem is this", which is what decides the right fix.
It fits the tab's notes onto the recording's real attacks and analyzes the drift curve:
• Progressive drift — the difference grows at a steady rate: the tab's tempo is not quite the recording's. Fixed with a new BPM, only on that stretch.
• Jump — the difference steps up: a bar too many/too few, a missing rest, a repeat. Never fixed with BPM — that would spread a local error across music that was correct.
• Structural difference — the tab's notes do not match the audio there; no timing correction solves it, the content is what is wrong.
Separate the instruments first: the notes are fitted onto the attacks of the isolated guitar, far more reliable than the mix.
Each finding is accepted or rejected individually and only goes into preview — "Apply and rebuild" is still what saves.
Honest limit: in a passage with a very regular rhythm, a bar too many/too few can be mathematically indistinguishable from missing notes — there you will see "synced" and unpaired notes, not a jump.
<p>O equivalente ao MIDI do RIPX, mas <b:
The equivalent of RIPX's MIDI, but done inside RockForge — without exporting anything from a DAW. It runs a neural beat detector (far more reliable than the normal automatic one on fast, dense music, where the classic detector gets the metrical level wrong) over the recording, detects the start of each bar and aligns each bar of the tab to that real time — the same anchor-per-bar as the MIDI tempo map.
Run "Separate instruments" first: detection is then done on the isolated drums (the cleanest beat signal); without separation it uses the full mix and warns you.
It respects Step 1 (it pins the 1st note, and the alignment grows from there) and stays in preview — review the ♩BPM per bar on the score and confirm with "Apply and rebuild".
Honest limit: it is a neural estimate, strong but not absolute truth like a RIPX MIDI checked by hand — if it fails on unusual material, import the MIDI. Requires the beatthis extra (Beat This! + torch); it can take a while.
<p>Quando a sincronização automática não:
When the automatic sync is not perfect, give it the truth instead of an estimate: a MIDI with the tempo per bar (exported from RIPX or any DAW from the same recording). Instead of guessing the tempo from the audio, RockForge reads the MIDI's tempo map and aligns each bar of the tab to its real time — one anchor per bar, the "BPM per bar".
It still respects Step 1: it pins the 1st note and the alignment grows from there. It stays in preview — review it on the score and confirm with "Apply and rebuild".
For it to work: the MIDI has to start at the tab's 1st bar (cut any intro the tab does not have) and have the same bar structure. The accuracy is that of RIPX's detection. PPQ format only (the usual one).

<p><strong>Arrastar nota:</strong> arras:
Drag note: drag a note horizontally to the right instant — it creates a correction point; the notes between points are stretched/compressed.

Snap to beats: with snapping on, the note jumps from beat to beat (the score's grid, shown with marks in the background) instead of sliding continuously. Hold Alt while dragging to place it freely (sub-beat fine-tuning). Choose "Playback cursor" in the grid to drag the note straight to the playhead's current position (instead of the nearest beat) — the most reliable way to line up with the cursor.

Mark at cursor: click a note to anchor it at the playback cursor's current position — handy for aligning while the audio plays.

Select excerpt: drag a box over the notes and then drag one of them — the excerpt moves as a block (also snapping to beats).

Move following: pause the audio at the right instant and click the displaced note — that note and all the following ones shift as a block to the cursor.

New beat (detect): click a note where the tempo changes — RockForge measures the recording's tempo from that instant and re-spaces the following notes.

Align bar: pause the recording where a bar should sound and click a note — a popup opens with the bar number (the note's own, already chosen). Confirm with "= cursor" and that bar lines up with the cursor, dragging the following notes along; or "= track" to align it to the same bar of another track that is already synced. Done several times along the song, it fixes the drift bar by bar.

Section: click a note to name where a section starts (intro/verse/chorus…) — nothing to do with sync, it is just the song's structure. See the "🏷️ Sections" panel below.

Edit notes: click an existing note to edit it (fret, sustain, techniques, bend, slide) or remove it; double-click on empty staff inserts a new note, snapped to the sync grid (a single click on empty space moves the cursor, as in the other modes). It changes the score's content — the notes no longer come only from the Guitar Pro file — and stays pending (dashed teal outline) until "Apply and rebuild".

<p>Define os tons da CDLC com <strong>ge:
Define the CDLC's tones with real gear (amplifier, cabinet and pedals/racks from the Rocksmith library). They are written into rockforge.rs2dlc and the .psarc, so they work in the game without you having to recreate them in DLC Builder.

Create: click "+ Create / edit tones", then "+ New tone". Choose the amplifier and the cabinet (required) and add optional effects. Each knob comes with the catalogue's default value.

Assign: choose the Base tone (the one that plays at the start) and tick up to 4 "extra" tones you can switch to along the song.

Switch midway: with the "Tone change" mode on, click a note on the score to place a switch to one of the extra tones there.

Per track: in the game, tones are per arrangement. With "Same tones on all tracks" ticked, they all use the same set; unticked, each track (the one open on the score) has its own base tone, extras and switches — the Lead can go to a solo tone while the Rhythm stays on crunch. The tones you create are shared.

They only apply to Guitar Pro projects. With no tones defined, DLC Builder flags "tone missing" and you fix it with its library.
<p>O \"Detetar tom\" mede o som da guita:
"Detect tone" measures the guitar's sound along the song (4 s windows): where it is cleanest, where it distorts most. Here, that sound is read against what each track plays in each part (the song's sections, or groups of 8 bars):

  • Clean — the recording is clean there, or the track lets chords/arpeggios ring without palm mute;
  • Solo — single notes with bends, vibrato, slurs or at fret 12 and up;
  • Rhythm — chords, palm mute.

For each part it picks the closest tone of that family, and says why and with what confidence. A part where the track does not play keeps the previous tone; consecutive parts with the same tone merge; each track ends up with at most 4 tones (Rocksmith's A–D slots, with the base included so it can switch back to it).

Honest limits: the separation gives ALL the guitars together, so the difference between tracks comes from the score, not the audio. The tones are chosen by character (distortion, brightness, low end) — they do not identify the real amplifier. The parts and times are those of the last rebuild.
